Thursday 9/17/2026 p.m.
Markets rebound as yields and oil pull back –
U.S. equity markets closed higher on Thursday as lower bond yields and oil prices helped boost investor sentiment. The 10-year Treasury yield declined to about 4.93%. Internationally, Asia finished mixed overnight, while European equities advanced after the Bank of England left its policy rate unchanged at 3.75%, as widely expected. In energy markets, WTI crude fell to about $101 per barrel amid reports that Saudi Arabia could bring additional supply to global markets through alternative export routes. The U.S. dollar weakened modestly against most major currencies, consistent with the drop in Treasury yields.
Jobless claims fall to two-year low –
Initial jobless claims declined to 196,000 this past week, compared with expectations to hold steady at 206,000. Continuing claims, which measure the total number of people receiving unemployment benefits, also fell to 1.73 million, below forecasts for 1.77 million and the lowest reading since January 2024. Together, the figures suggest that layoffs remain limited and labor-market conditions are relatively healthy. Continued resilience in employment should help support household income and consumer spending, while giving the Fed greater flexibility to remain focused on inflation.
Housing starts weaken more than expected –
Privately owned housing starts fell in August to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.27 million, below estimates of roughly 1.32 million. Building permits, a forward-looking indicator of construction activity, were issued at an annualized pace of about 1.39 million, also falling short of forecasts. The weakness suggests homebuilders are becoming more cautious as elevated mortgage rates weigh on housing demand. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate has risen to 6.95% in recent months, broadly tracking the increase in 10-year Treasury yields. Pending home sales rose by 0.3% month-over-month in August, missing expectations for a 0.5% increase and pointing to continued softness in the housing market. With both starts and permits weakening, residential construction activity could contribute less to economic growth in the near term. Over time, however, softer housing demand may help moderate home-price growth and rent pressures, contributing to slower shelter inflation.
Brian Therien, CFA

CNBC Reporter & Morning Squawk Writer
Happy Thursday. Breaking news this morning: Nvidia has agreed to buy open-source artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face
for nearly $13 billion.
Stock futures
are mixed this morning after a
winning day
on Wall Street.
Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day:
1. Summit up
The G20 wrapped up its two-day Innovation Ministerial yesterday, where technology leaders and government representatives talked artificial intelligence, data centers and tariffs.
Here are some of the biggest headlines out of the gathering:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that AI will “democratize intelligence” for G20 countries and called the technology “the great equalizer.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, meanwhile, said using AI is a “non-negotiable” for countries, comparing the adoption of AI to the adoption of electricity.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp acknowledged that there are “huge dangers” to the technology but pushed back on what he called the “doom message” around AI. He appeared to allude to Anthropic and its CEO, who have warned about the technology’s risks.
On the data center front, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown said he “really loved” President Donald Trump’s Monday Truth Social post, in which the president said communities who opposed data centers “want to end up being backwards and poor.”
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said that data centers will “bring prosperity” and are “getting a bad rap.” He also downplayed the facilities’ water consumption.
Catch up on all the biggest moments here.
2. Bond, John Bond
After hitting its
highest level since 2023
, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield pulled back in Wednesday’s session, providing relief for other corners of the market.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams told CNBC yesterday that the recent yield jumps should be seen as
a sign of a strong economy
rather than as market dysfunction. Williams also said he would have to “wait and see” before deciding whether an interest rate hike would be necessary to calm inflation.
The three major averages snapped three-day losing streaks yesterday.
Follow live market updates here.
